responses.mission_1.search: BFS and A* both found a shortest path of 13.5 m. BFS expanded 928 nodes, while A* expanded 700 nodes, so A* examined 228 fewer cells. My BFS implementation uses a FIFO queue to explore cells in layers. My A* implementation uses a heap ordered by the cost so far plus the Manhattan-distance heuristic, which helps guide the search toward the goal. However, A* took about 9.34 ms, compared with 6.99 ms for BFS. Examining fewer cells did not make it faster in this run.
responses.mission_1.failure:
On the constrained map, BFS found a 24.5 m path and expanded 848 nodes. DFS found a much longer 104 m path but expanded only 524 nodes. My DFS implementation uses a stack and follows deeper branches first, so it can reach the goal without finding the shortest route. IDDFS reached the expansion budget and returned resource_limit. On the unreachable map, BFS, DFS, IDDFS, and A all returned no_path. This means they exhausted the search without finding a route. In contrast, resource_limit means the search stopped because it reached a time limit.
I used AI to help with the writing of the four implementations, and I ran the full evaluation and inspected the resulting metrics and route plots.
responses.mission_2.prediction: I predict the robot will reach the goal sooner with A* than with DFS on the constrained map. A* uses the distance traveled so far and the estimated distance to the goal to guide its search. DFS follows one branch at a time and can end up with a winding route. In Mission 1, A* found a 24.5 m route on the constrained map, while DFS found a 104 m route. The robot will have to slow down for turns around the walls, but with the same controller and speed limit, I expect A*’s shorter route to take less time to drive.
responses.mission_2.performance: Yes. On the constrained map, A* succeeded in 90.19 simulated seconds after driving 23.91 m. DFS timed out after 180.44 simulated seconds and drove 44.08 m. At checkpoint 1760, the DFS trajectory ends near the bottom of the map, still 7.33 m from the goal. Its planned route was 104 m long, compared with 24.5 m for A*. That helps explain why DFS drove farther than A* and still ran out of time. The elapsed-time gap was larger on the open map, about 133 seconds versus 90 seconds on the constrained map. Both DFS times show when the trial stopped.
responses.mission_2.choice: I would choose Nav2 Smac 2D because it completed both deliveries in the least driving time in my trials. It succeeded in 35.12 seconds on the open map and 73.75 seconds on the constrained map. A* also succeeded on both, but Nav2 drove 10.06 m versus A*’s 13.15 m on the open map, and 20.64 m versus 23.91 m on the constrained map. For a delivery, the advantage I care about most is reaching the destination sooner.
responses.mission_3.prediction: On the open map, both social settings produced complete preview paths that moved slightly farther away from the person than the baseline. On the constrained map, social_1 produced a complete path, while social_2 got stuck and oscillated near the person and wall. Social_2 used a higher repulsion strength and a larger influence distance, so I cannot tell from this comparison which change caused the oscillation.
responses.mission_3.comparison: For A*, social_2 had the largest minimum person clearance at 0.841 m, compared with 0.725 m for the baseline. Time inside the 0.75 m personal-space threshold fell from 1.6 seconds to 0 seconds. The social_2 run took 46.90 seconds, compared with 46.54 seconds for the baseline, an increase of about 0.36 seconds. For RRT, the baseline had the largest minimum clearance at 1.742 m. Both social_1 and social_2 were slightly lower, at 1.731 m and 1.729 m. All three RRT conditions spent 0 seconds inside the personal-space threshold. In these runs, the baseline already left substantial space around the person, and neither social setting increased its measured minimum clearance.
responses.mission_3.recommendation:
I would keep the RRT baseline for this scenario. It succeeded with a minimum person clearance of 1.742 m and took 43.83 simulated seconds. As an alternative, A* with social_2 also succeeded, but its minimum clearance was 0.841 m and it took 46.90 seconds. Both spent zero recorded seconds inside the 0.75 m threshold.

These results come from one trial per condition with a static simulated person. They cannot tell us how the robot would respond to someone walking
responses.final.synthesis:
A good route should be reasonable for the planner to find, practical for the robot to follow, and give people enough space. In Mission 1, A* found a 13.5 m route on the open map while examining fewer cells than BFS. In Mission 2, A* reached the goal on both maps, while DFS timed out on both after following much longer routes.
In Mission 3, A* with the stronger social field increased the estimated minimum clearance from 0.725 m to 0.841 m and spent less time close to the person while the RRT already left more space.
responses.final.course_reflection:
This lab showed me how a robot finds its way around and how it Plans a route and choses different algorithms.
The simulations took a while to run, but comparing the results helped me understand why different planning methods can lead to different outcomes.
